idiom_name: include Comparable and define <=> (plus Struct/Data for value semantics)
implementation_notes: Ruby's Comparable module is the mixin form of this pattern: include it, define <=> (returning -1, 0, +1, or nil when the operands are not comparable), and the module supplies #<, #<=, #==, #>=, #>, #between? and #clamp for the class - one primitive operation, the whole operator family, no per-type operator code. It deliberately does not supply eql? or hash, so hash-key behaviour still needs those, and Struct/Data.define generate value equality for simple value types. Because Ruby resolves at runtime, the 'family' is exactly the set of classes that include the module: there is no compile-time injection to reason about, and monkey-patching a comparable class affects every instance.
code_sketch:
class Version
  include Comparable            # brings <, <=, ==, >=, >, between?, clamp
  attr_reader :major, :minor
  def initialize(major, minor)
    @major, @minor = major, minor
  end
  def <=>(other)                # the only primitive you write
    [major, minor] <=> [other.major, other.minor]
  end
end
Version.new(1, 2) < Version.new(1, 10)   # => true
pitfalls: Comparable#== is derived from <=> and is not the same as eql?/hash, so hash lookups can disagree with the comparison operators if those are not defined consistently.
<=> must return nil (not false, not raise) for incomparable operands; otherwise comparisons raise 'comparison of X with Y failed' at the call site - a common bug when mixing units or numeric types.

Including Comparable where a superclass or refinement already defines the operators changes behaviour for the whole class at runtime, and re-including it to 'fix' semantics can silently reorder existing collections.
